schools.summary: Henry holds that Moses saw and heard very glorious things in the cloud which it was not lawful nor possible to utter, and that he therefore recorded nothing to satisfy the curiosity of those who would intrude into what they have not seen, but only what he was to speak to the children of Israel, since Scripture is designed to direct us in our duty and not to fill our heads with speculations.

Keil and Delitzsch give the purpose of the building, to give a definite external form to the covenant and construct a visible bond of fellowship, and argue that its erection could not be left to the inventive faculty of any man but must proceed from him who was there to manifest himself as the Holy One in righteousness and grace, so that the people could only carry out what God appointed.

Gill fixes the two moments the verse holds apart, that the Lord spake to Moses when on the mount and in the midst of the cloud, and that the speaking to Israel was to come when he should go down from the mountain to the camp.
Wesley repeats the judgement about what Moses withheld almost word for word, and adds that probably no house or temple was ever built for sacred uses before this tabernacle.

debates.question: Why was the sanctuary to be built at all?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch answer from the covenant, that it was to give the covenant a definite external form and a visible bond of fellowship; Henry answers from kingship, that God had chosen this people as a peculiar people and would be their King, and having already given them laws now orders a royal palace set up among them, at once ceremonial and typical.

outliers.view: Reads the silence of the record as a rule for Scripture itself, that what Moses saw in the cloud was left unwritten because the Bible is given to direct us in our duty rather than to satisfy curiosity.

themes: let them make me a sanctuary

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that God prefaced his directions about materials and form by inviting the people to contribute from their stores, calls the erection of sanctuaries one of the fittest occasions for man to show gratitude by giving to God of his own, gives the Hebrew as of every man whose heart impels him, and states bluntly that unless gifts come from the heart they are an offence to God.

Clarke explains the term as a kind of free-will offering consisting of anything necessary for the occasion, properly meaning anything lifted up since in presenting it to God it was lifted up to be laid on his altar, and supplies the political sense, that God required a tent suited in some sort to his dignity because he was to act as their king; Wesley notes that it was not prescribed what or how much they must give but left to their generosity.

Calvin spends his longest note here on the date rather than the offering, answering an opinion that the tabernacle was built and set up before Moses brought down the first tables, and rejecting it on three grounds of chronology and arrangement.
Henry insists the gifts came not by a tax imposed upon them but by a voluntary contribution.

debates.question: Was the tabernacle erected before or after Moses received the first tables?
debates.positions: Calvin reports three arguments for the earlier date, from a tabernacle named immediately after the tables were broken, from a testimony not yet received being ordered into the ark, and from the silence about the apostasy when the people are exhorted to build; he answers that the tent there was Moses own and pitched outside the host, that what was described first was the form the ark should take rather than the ark, and that the silence is forbearance rather than innocence. His own three reasons are that the form was shown during the forty days at the end of which the tables were given, that the tabernacle was reared in the first month of the second year with the camp removing a month and a half later, leaving no room for two further absences of forty days, and that the earlier dating would require transposing a great part of the book.

outliers.view: Turns the qualifying clause into a rule about giving in general, that gifts which do not come from the heart are an offence to God, who loveth a cheerful giver.

themes: that they bring me an offering
of every man that giveth it willingly

schools.summary: Gill reads the list as a list of alternatives rather than a schedule of dues, since it was not expected that something of each should be had of everyone but that every man should give whatever suited him best to bestow, and notes that many were supplied for the service out of what they had brought from Egypt, so that having had the riches by God giving them favour in the eyes of the Egyptians they were under the greater obligation to part with some of it freely; Calvin draws the moral of the variety rather than of the quantity, that what the poor offer of their little is not eclipsed by the abundance of the rich, since God reckons goats hair among the sacred offerings not less than gold.

Clarke distinguishes four Hebrew words for gold and assigns each a stage, gold in the ore, gold coined and stamped, wrought and polished gold used for gilding, and gold formed into plate, holding that the third is the word here because it was in a state capable of being manufactured for the sanctuary; he derives silver from a root meaning pale or white and takes brass for copper unless the factitious metal is meant.

Ellicott asks whether they could afford it and answers that they could, having brought out of Egypt both their ancestral wealth and the gifts received at their departure and added the plunder of the Amalekites, while the silver was comparatively small and the brass, or rather bronze, since brass seems to have been unknown at this time, was of no great value.

debates.question: What does the variety of the materials mean?
debates.positions: Calvin makes it a picture of the Church, that by the varied and manifold contributions God would show as in a glass that a variety of gifts are necessary to the building of the spiritual temple, and that those who aid the Church by their more excellent gifts should admit poor brethren into fellowship without contempt; Gill keeps to the practical point, that each gave what he had and what he had a heart to give; Clarke and Ellicott attend only to the metals themselves.

outliers.view: Finds the doctrine in the mixture rather than the value, that as gold and precious stones were mixed with brass and iron in the one building, so the more richly gifted are to receive the poor into fellowship without dislike.

themes: what the poor offer of their little

schools.summary: Gill is careful that what was asked for was a cloth and not a colour, since the Jewish doctors are much divided about these words but by them we are to understand neither the colours themselves, which could not be brought, nor the materials for dyeing them, but wool or cloths of those colours made up into yarn and woven, much used in the garments of the priests, the curtains and the vail.

Clarke works from philology and the poets, taking the first colour for an azure or sky colour rendered by the old versions a deep violet, the second for a very precious colour extracted from a shell-fish and supposed to be the famous Tyrian purple, and the third from a word signifying a worm joined to another signifying to double, which implies the cloth was twice dipped, whence the old rendering of scarlet twice dyed and the French and English words for crimson; on the goats hair he cites the poet who reckoned it nearly of equal value with wool; Wesley disposes of the whole clause in five words.

Ellicott names the sources instead, a dark blue from indigo which was the only blue known to the Egyptians, a purplish crimson from the murex which was the main source of the Tyrian dye, and a scarlet from the cochineal insect of the holm oak now superseded by the brighter tint from Mexico; the fine linen he settles from the mummy cloths as white thread spun from flax, and the goats hair from present practice, the covering of an Arab tent being to this day almost always of it.

debates.question: What were the three colours?
debates.positions: Clarke reasons from the words and the ancient dye-trade, an azure or violet, the Tyrian purple from a shell-fish, and a twice-dipped crimson; Ellicott reasons from the materials actually available in Egypt and names indigo, the murex and the cochineal insect; they arrive close together by different evidence.

debates.question: What is the fine linen?
debates.positions: Clarke reports that whether the word means linen, cotton or silk is not agreed among interpreters, and gives the rabbinic derivation from the word for six, the fine linen of Egypt in which six folds constituted one thread; Ellicott answers from the mummy cloths and other undyed fabrics that it is white thread spun from flax, yellowish white, soft and wonderfully fine.

outliers.view: Supports the value of goats hair cloth from a Latin poet, who has the shepherd shearing the hoary beards of the herd to make cloth warm in tents for the soldier and a shield for the shivering mariner.

schools.summary: Clarke defends the literal red rams from natural history, that many travellers attest sheep in the Levant with red or violet fleeces and that almost all ancient writers say the same, one describing the rams of Polyphemus so, from which facts he thinks the fable of the golden fleece very probably arose; on the second kind of skin he follows the scholar who seems to have proved that no animal is intended but a colour, none of the ancient versions acknowledging an animal except the Chaldee from which our badger is borrowed; and he argues the wood is the acacia from its being plentiful in Egypt and abundant in the very desert where Moses built.

Ellicott looks to the tanneries for the red skins, North Africa having always been celebrated for the best leather and its red skins famous in all ages, objects that the badger is native neither to North Africa nor to the Arabian desert so that the rendering is a very improbable conjecture, and reports the Arabic word as naming a marine animal resembling the seal; Keil and Delitzsch settle on the sea-cow of the Red Sea and note that its upper skin would serve for the thick covering of tents and the under for ornamental sandals.

Calvin quotes the naturalists on the acacia and adds that the most important material, the wood for the tent, is just the one found there most plentifully, and that the Greek translators named it wood that never decays.

debates.question: Does the second kind of skin name an animal or a colour?
debates.positions: Clarke follows the scholar who holds it a colour, a very deep blue, and marshals the old versions, which give violet, azure, black and simply ram-skins; Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep the animal but move it into the sea, to a seal or dugong or, for Keil and Delitzsch specifically, the sea-cow of the Red Sea whose skin is admirably adapted for sandals.

debates.question: What tree is the shittah?
debates.positions: Clarke reports it supposed by some the finest kind of cedar and by others the acacia, and argues for the acacia from supply; Ellicott treats the identification as settled, since there are no trees in that region from which boards could be cut except the palm and the acacia, and answers the objection that the tree is now too small there by noting that it grows larger further north.

outliers.view: Adds his own field observation to the ancient testimony, sheep he has seen in the Zetland Isles with fleeces white, black and chocolate.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the clauses about oil and spices as assumptions carried forward, that the sanctuary will need lighting, that anointing oil will be needed with spices as an ingredient since the tabernacle and its vessels and its priests had to be consecrated by anointing, and that there would be incense to burn; on the stones he counts the disagreement among the old versions and concludes plainly that there is considerable doubt what stone is meant, adding that only three were required, one for the breastplate and two for the shoulder-pieces; Keil and Delitzsch prefer beryls, gloss the second phrase as stones of filling, and record that the precious stones were presented by the princes of the congregation.

Clarke raises the practical objection that the oil must have been brought from Egypt since there were no olives in the wilderness, half answers it by supposing these directions look forward to a fixed and settled residence, and gives a long description of the ephod while admitting at the outset that it is very difficult to tell what it was or in what form it was made.

Gill derives the name of the stone from its likeness to the nail of a man finger and lists the competing renderings, beryl in the old versions, sardius in the Greek, and sardonyx in the judgement of those who think it had a likeness both to the onyx and to the sardius.

debates.question: What stone is meant?
debates.positions: Gill, Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke all confess uncertainty and answer differently: Gill lists beryl, sardius and sardonyx without choosing; Ellicott states flatly that there is considerable doubt; Keil and Delitzsch prefer beryls; Clarke guesses at the fine pale stone called the Egyptian pebble, specimens of which lay before him from his own collection of minerals.

debates.question: What was the ephod?
debates.positions: Clarke offers two guesses and prefers the second: first, following the root meaning to bind close, a kind of girdle brought over the shoulders, crossed on the stomach and carried round the waist; then a garment like that worn by heralds, covering back, breast and belly, open at the sides and probably without sleeves.

outliers.view: Note that the word rendered sweet incense means literally the scents, because the materials of which it was composed were not all of them fragrant.

themes: stones to be set in the ephod

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the sentence the point the whole list has been running toward, the enumeration of the gifts having been subordinate to it; he explains why the house had to be a tent, since a people without fixed abode and continually shifting quarters must soon have quitted a building or forgone their hopes of Palestine, so that God devised a tent-temple modelled on the better Oriental tents but of the best materials and still portable; and he will not let the caution about dwelling empty the promise, since God manifested himself sensibly in the Holy of Holies where he dwelt continually.

Calvin holds that the promise is what moves the giving, since no one willingly deprives himself of his own unless he has some compensation in view, and then guards the promise itself, that he who sits above the heavens could not be enclosed in the tabernacle, and that it was not the infinite essence of God that dwelt there but his name, or the record of his name; Gill defines the word simply as a holy place to dwell in, so called from his dwelling in it.

Clarke narrows the word to that part of the tabernacle called the most holy place, into which the high priest entered only once a year on the great day of atonement; Wesley compresses the whole caution into a clause, that it is not by his essence, which is everywhere, but by his grace and glorious operations.

debates.question: In what sense could God dwell there?
debates.positions: Calvin and Wesley guard the word against the letter, Calvin insisting that not the infinite essence but the name of God dwelt there and Wesley that it is by grace and glorious operations rather than by essence; Ellicott makes the same concession and then refuses to let it empty the promise, since God manifested himself sensibly in the Holy of Holies and might be consulted there by the temporal ruler of the nation.

outliers.view: Explains the form of the building from the condition of the people, that a nomadic nation would have had to abandon a permanent structure or abandon its hopes of Palestine, so that a portable tent-temple was devised in harmony with their condition.

themes: let them make me a sanctuary
that I may dwell among them
not his essence but his name

schools.summary: Ellicott states the question as a choice of three, whether God showed Moses a material structure furnished with material objects, a pictorial representation of the whole, or a series of visions in which the forms were represented to the eye of the mind, and judges the entire analogy of the divine dealings to be in favour of the last; Keil and Delitzsch argue a narrower question of tense against those who take the showing as already finished, holding that the participle does not refer to the past and that nothing in the later expression implies Moses had left the mountain.

Gill reads the clause as an instruction about workmanship, that the sanctuary was to be made exactly according to the view Moses had upon the mount, which he was to communicate to the workmen for their instruction and direction; Calvin hears a prohibition in it as much as a direction, that the artificers should not dare to invent anything, since it would be a profanation to mix up anything human with the commands of God.

Wesley turns the minuteness of the instructions into an argument about Scripture itself, that Moses gave a very short and general account of the creation of the world but describes the tabernacle with the greatest niceness and accuracy imaginable, because God church and instituted religion is more precious to him than all the rest of the world; Clarke reports an older opinion that there had been a tabernacle before the one Moses erected, and glosses the word as meaning literally the dwelling or habitation.

debates.question: What kind of thing was the pattern?
debates.positions: Ellicott sets out three possibilities, a material model, a picture, or a vision, and prefers the vision on the analogy of the divine dealings; Clarke assumes a material original, an ancient tabernacle on which the new one was to be modelled; Keil and Delitzsch do not answer the question but insist on the tense, that the showing is not spoken of as already past.

outliers.view: Argues from the disproportion between the two accounts, that the creation of the world is described in a few general words while the tabernacle is described with the greatest niceness, because Scripture was written to acquaint us with the methods of grace rather than the works of nature.

themes: according to all that I shew thee
after the pattern of the tabernacle
the pattern of all the instruments

schools.summary: Ellicott insists on the word, that the term rendered ark here is entirely different from the one used of the vessel that rode the flood and of the basket among the reeds, and properly means a chest or coffer of small dimensions used to contain valuables, once even applied to a mummy-case; he places the object in its setting, sacred coffers being important parts of the furniture of Egyptian temples; and on the overlaying he weighs gilding against plating and prefers plating as simpler in the desert and thought more suitable because more valuable; Keil and Delitzsch call the crown a golden rim encircling the ark like an ornamental wreath.

Henry marks its place in the design, the ark with its appurtenances being the furniture of the most holy place and the special token of God presence, for which the tabernacle was erected to be the receptacle, and converts the dimensions on a cubit of twenty-one inches.

Clarke ranges the word over ark, chest, coffer and coffin, judges the ark the most excellent of all the holy things of the Mosaic economy for whose sake the tabernacle and temple were built, and reasons backwards from the box to the tables it was to hold, that their length was not less than four feet and their breadth not less than two; Wesley repeats Henry figures exactly.

Gill reads the material for what it signifies, the wood being incorruptible and rendered in the Greek by a word meaning exactly that, which he takes to denote the perpetuity of Christ in his person and in the natures united in it, and he states plainly that the ark was not gilded but had a plate of pure gold put over it.

debates.question: How large was the ark?
debates.positions: Henry and Wesley make it about fifty-two inches by thirty-one by thirty-one on a cubit of twenty-one inches; Clarke on the same cubit gives four feet five by two feet six by two feet six; Ellicott gives three feet nine by two feet three by two feet three — three conversions of the same figures that agree within inches.

debates.question: Was the ark gilded or plated?
debates.positions: Ellicott allows gilding to be possible but scarcely probable, since it requires much apparatus and was less likely in the desert than the simpler method of overlaying with plates, which would also be thought more valuable, and notes the Jewish tradition for plates; Gill states the same conclusion flatly.

outliers.view: Infers the size of the tables of stone from the size of the box made to hold them, and declines to guess their thickness because the ark was meant for other things besides, the rod and the pot of manna, which he thinks were probably laid beside it rather than in it.

themes: they shall make an ark of shittim wood
a crown of gold round about

schools.summary: Ellicott explains both the number of the rings and their odd position, that the four were made to receive the two poles by which the ark was to be borne on the shoulders of the priests, and that the Hebrew is literally at the four feet, so that the rings went at the bottom corners and not the top in order that the ark might be elevated above the bearers and never come into contact with their persons; he grants the objection about equilibrium and answers it from the smallness of the dimensions, and he reads the standing order about the poles as a matter of danger, that there might never be a necessity for touching the ark itself, since he who touched it imperilled his life; Keil and Delitzsch translate the word for the feet as walking feet, bent as if for walking.

Clarke reads the same order as readiness rather than danger, the ark being always to be considered as in readiness to be removed since God had not told them at what hour he would command them to strike their tents; and he raises against himself the difficulty that another passage speaks of putting in the staves when the camp set forward, answering with a great show of probability that besides the poles in the rings there were two others in the form of a bier, taken from under the ark when they encamped.

Gill attends to the making rather than the placing, that a mould was made and the melted gold poured into it, that the poles were of the same wood as the ark and covered so that they appeared all of gold, and that the poles were not only to be put into the rings but to remain in them, yea, always.

debates.question: Why were the rings set at the feet rather than the corners?
debates.positions: Ellicott answers that the ark was to ride above the bearers shoulders and never touch them, and meets the objection that this would endanger its equilibrium by citing the smallness of its dimensions; Keil and Delitzsch describe the feet without arguing the point.

debates.question: Were the poles ever removed?
debates.positions: Clarke states the difficulty that another passage seems to require their removal when the camp encamped, and reconciles it by supposing a second pair of poles in the form of a bier which were withdrawn while the ark own poles stayed in their rings; Ellicott and Gill simply insist that they always remained.

outliers.view: Grounds the whole arrangement in a danger rather than in convenience, that the poles stayed in place so that there might never be any necessity for touching the ark, since he who touched it imperilled his life.

themes: they shall not be taken from it

schools.summary: Calvin holds that the title so often given to the law indicates something more than the rule of a just and holy life, namely the compact whereby God bound himself to his people and his people to himself, the word being equivalent to a contract or convention, and carries the point through the Psalms, where the name is given not only to the Commandments but to whatever God delivered by the hand of Moses; Gill makes it a testification of the mind and will of God, what he would have done or omitted, which would stand as a testimony against the Israelites should they transgress what they had approved, and follows the deposit into its application to Christ.
Ellicott keeps the narrower sense, calling it simply God witness against sin, and notes the consequence for the chest, that as containing the tables it was called the ark of the testimony.

Clarke notes that the tables were not yet given, derives the word from a root meaning forward or onward, to bear witness to or of a person or thing, and widens the witness to everything the ark held, the rod and the pot of manna and the holy anointing oil bearing testimony to the Messiah in his prophetic, sacerdotal and regal offices.

debates.question: How much is contained in the word testimony?
debates.positions: Calvin presses it furthest, to a covenant and a contract, so that the table of the covenant is afterwards used instead of the testimony and the law and the testimony named together are not two things but one commended twice; Gill and Ellicott keep the narrower sense of a witness to the will of God and against sin; Clarke widens it in a different direction, to every object the ark contained.

outliers.view: Follows the deposit through to its application, that the law laid up inside the ark may signify that the law was in the heart of Christ, which he undertook to fulfil and with pleasure did.

themes: the testimony which I shall give thee

schools.summary: Ellicott names the parties to the dispute and decides it, granting that the simple verb has the physical meaning of covering but insisting that the intensive form has never any other meaning than covering or expiating sins and that the noun is formed from the intensive, so that the old Greek and Latin renderings and our mercy seat are correct; Keil and Delitzsch argue the same case, that the meaning lid cannot be sustained since the verb has not the literal sense of covering in either conjugation, and both call decisive the passage naming the holy of holies the house of expiation.

Calvin concedes the philology to the other side and then declines the conclusion, doubting not that Moses alludes to a metaphorical meaning since the law requires a covering to conceal our transgressions, and arguing from the furniture rather than the grammar that it is a tame explanation to make it a mere lid when the cherubim turn their faces toward it and God promises to answer from it; Gill keeps both senses without choosing and notes that the old Greek version renders it the propitiatory covering.

Clarke reaches the sense by the metaphor itself, that by an act of pardon sins are represented as covered so that they no longer appear in the eye of divine justice, and records that the high priest sprinkled the blood of the expiatory sacrifices here on the great day of atonement; Wesley states the figure in a line, a type of Christ the great propitiation whose satisfaction covers our transgressions.

debates.question: Does the word mean a lid or a propitiatory?
debates.positions: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch decide for propitiatory on the form of the verb, and both cite the place where the holy of holies is called the house of expiation as decisive against the covering-house; Calvin grants their philology and argues from the honours paid to the object that the plain lid is too tame a reading; Gill declines to choose and keeps both senses, as he says the old Greek version did.

outliers.view: Reckons the cost of the object, a solid mass of pure gold rather than plated wood, at seven hundred and fifty pounds Troy and above twenty-five thousand pounds in value, the outlay marking it as the crowning glory of the material tabernacle.

themes: a mercy seat of pure gold

schools.summary: Clarke says outright that what these were we cannot distinctly say, reports the general supposition of a creature with four heads and one body drawn from the noblest of their kinds so that they might be representatives of all nature, and adds that the term often means a figure of any kind, such as was sculptured on stone or embroidered on cloth.

Ellicott sets out three schools, those who take them for winged bulls not unlike the Assyrian, those who regard them as more composite like the Egyptian sphinxes, and the predominant opinion which he follows, that they were simply human figures with the addition of a pair of wings, resembling the figures often seen inside Egyptian arks.

Gill rejects a string of identifications rather than proposing a form, denying that they are emblems of the two Testaments or of the angels or of the persons of the Godhead and making them emblems of the saints of both dispensations; Calvin takes the opposite side of that question and is content with less, preferring the derivation that treats the word as meaning any image at all and holding it enough that the images were winged and represented angels.
Wesley agrees that they represent the holy angels, not by any effigy of an angel but by some emblem of the angelical nature.

debates.question: What did a cherub look like?
debates.positions: Clarke refuses to say and reports the composite creature of four heads; Ellicott lists winged bulls, sphinx-like composites and winged human figures, and follows the last as the predominant opinion; Calvin refuses the question as unimportant, holding it enough that the images were winged and represented angels.

debates.question: What did the cherubim stand for?
debates.positions: Gill denies that they are the angels, since the two are distinguished, and makes them the saints of both dispensations; Calvin and Wesley make them the angels, Calvin because God appointed angels, by whom he exercises his dominion, to be a symbol of his presence.

outliers.view: Refuses the reading that makes the word mean like a boy, calling it forced and refuted by the prophet who gives the same name to the forms of a calf, a lion and an eagle as well as to the human form.

themes: in the two ends of the mercy seat

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses the beaten work as not cast but brought into shape by the hammer, notes that the Egyptian word for to hammer is the one from which some derive the name cherub, explains that the figures were not detached images fastened on but formed out of the same mass of gold, and observes that both wings of both figures were to be elevated and advanced so as to overshadow and protect the mercy seat, unlike the Egyptian figures in which one wing is depressed; Keil and Delitzsch describe the posture exactly, a screen formed over the covering with the faces turned towards one another but inclining towards it.

Gill reads the outstretched wings as evidence about the shape, that they were winged creatures like the seraphim and living creatures of the prophets, with wings stretched upward towards the heaven above their heads rather than hanging at their sides, and notes that there was one at each end and not two at both; Calvin refuses the obvious inference from the covering, holding that they covered the lid not to hide it but to mark the readiness of their obedience, the extension of the wings being equivalent to being prepared to perform whatever God might command.

Wesley gathers the whole posture into a sentence and reads it, that the faces looked one towards another and both downwards towards the ark while the wings were stretched out so as to touch, which notes their attendance upon the Redeemer, their readiness to do his will, their presence in the assemblies of saints and their desire to look into the mysteries of the gospel.

debates.question: Why were the wings spread over the covering?
debates.positions: Ellicott takes it as overshadowing and, as it were, protection; Calvin denies that concealment is meant and makes the outstretched wings a figure of readiness to perform whatever God commands; Wesley reads both wings and faces as attendance upon the Redeemer and desire to look into the mysteries of the gospel; Keil and Delitzsch describe the screen without assigning it a meaning.

outliers.view: Reads the faces turned towards each other as a figure of the harmony in which the angels are united for performing the commands of God, and the faces turned towards the mercy seat as attentiveness to his will.

themes: stretch forth their wings on high
their faces shall look one to another

schools.summary: Gill reads the placing for its doctrine rather than its carpentry, that the mercy seat set above the ark where the law was signifies that there is no mercy but in a way of righteousness and of satisfaction to the law of God, the cherubim over it making a throne for the majesty of God and the ark below a kind of footstool, so that Christ stands between God and his law as mediator; and he widens the promised meeting beyond Moses to the high priest in later times and to the people of God as represented by him.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the posture of the cherubim by the promise that follows, and give the verb its precise force, to appoint, to present oneself to a person at an appointed place; Ellicott distinguishes two modes within the one promise, that God would meet his people there either literally, as when he answered inquiries of the high priest, or spiritually, as when he accepted incense and the blood of offerings and prayers offered through the priests, and draws from the promise the name of the whole building, the Tent of Meeting, which our version renders less happily as the tabernacle of the congregation.

Clarke keeps to the place and the occasion, that it was over the mercy seat and between the cherubim that God chose to give the most especial manifestations of himself, where the divine glory was to be seen and where Moses was to come to consult him about the management of the people.

debates.question: What kind of meeting was promised?
debates.positions: Clarke keeps it concrete, a place where the divine glory was seen and where Moses came to consult God about the management of the people; Ellicott divides it into a literal mode, the answering of inquiries, and a spiritual one, the acceptance of incense and blood and prayer; Gill extends the parties to the high priest and to the people he represented.

outliers.view: Closes with an application traced to the rabbis, that the heart of man may be likened to God sanctuary, so that as the divine glory dwelt where the ark and the tables and the cherubim were, a place should be made in the heart for the divine Majesty and be its holy of holies.

themes: put the mercy seat above upon the ark
there I will meet with thee

schools.summary: Gill argues from the logic of a house, that as the sanctuary was a house for God to dwell in he would have the proper furniture of a house, and fixes the table in the holy place on the north side rather than in the holy of holies where nothing but the ark stood; Calvin arrives at nearly the same place by way of an objection, and answers it from the difference of the dispensations, that God would have the loaves deposited among the golden dishes not because he had need of meat and drink but that he might prescribe the duty of temperance to his people by deigning to have his table among them.

Clarke quotes an older divine at length, that the mystery of the tabernacle was that it should be a place for the habitation of Divinity to be fixed in, and that once a dwelling is granted everything suitable to a house must follow, the table with its dishes though they were never used, the candlestick with its lamps continually burning, a continual fire on the altar as the focus of the house, and provision brought in by the sacrifices.

Henry works the image from the other end, that God kept a good house and that in a royal palace it was fit there should be a royal table, and gives the purpose of the bread under three heads, a thankful acknowledgement of daily bread, a token of communion since the loaves were of the same corn as the bread on their own tables, and a type of the spiritual provision made in the church by the gospel; Wesley repeats the reading closely.
Ellicott notes only that no other wood was to be employed, either for the sanctuary itself or for its furniture.

debates.question: Does God need a table?
debates.positions: Calvin raises the difficulty through the saying of an ancient bishop who sold the sacred vessels in a famine and excused himself on the ground that our God, who does not eat or drink, has no need of patens and chalices; he answers that the bishop spoke piously under the Gospel what would have been unseasonable under the Law, since at the coming of Christ the shadows of the Law ceased, and that the loaves were required not for God need but to teach the people temperance and to remind them that their food was taken as before God.

outliers.view: Reads the arrangement as hospitality rather than ritual, that the tabernacle being God house he would show that he kept a good house, and that God and Israel did as it were eat together, since the bread on his table was of the same corn as the bread on theirs.

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the practical reason for the plating and a classification with it, that like the ark and the altar of incense the table was to be overlaid with gold, being a species of altar on which lay offerings to God; he prefers a plainer word for the crown, an edging to prevent what was placed on the table from falling off; he settles the disputed band from a monument rather than a text, the representation on the Arch of Titus showing a flat bar midway between the top of the table and its feet, connecting the legs; and on the clause fixing where the rings went he admits that the meaning is not very clear; Keil and Delitzsch describe the same fittings and add that the vessels were to be of pure gold.

Gill says the table was covered with a plate of gold so that the wood was not seen and takes it to denote the excellency of Christ human nature or rather of his divine nature, reports that the Jewish teachers are divided about the band, some placing it above and some below with the board laid upon it, offers the old versions which render the preposition as under rather than over against, and says of the poles only that they were made in like manner as those for the ark.

debates.question: Where did the band round the table run?
debates.positions: Gill reports the Jewish teachers divided, some putting it above and round the table and others below, fixed from foot to foot with the board laid on it; Ellicott decides from the carving on the Arch of Titus that it was a flat bar midway between the top and the feet, connecting the four legs, and holds its golden edging to have been only ornament.

debates.question: What does over against the border mean?
debates.positions: Ellicott concedes the meaning is not very clear, since if the framing had been at the bottom of the legs the rings could have been opposite where it was inserted, whereas the framing appears to have been halfway up while the rings were at the bottom, so that they were opposite it only in a loose and vague sense; Gill gives the old versions, which read under rather than over against, and the rabbinic view that the rings were fixed to the feet opposite the top of the band.

outliers.view: Settles two disputed fittings from a Roman monument rather than from the text, reading both the band and the height at which the table was carried off the carving on the Arch of Titus.

themes: a border of an hand breadth
that the table may be borne

schools.summary: Clarke guesses at the four vessels one by one from their roots, the dishes for the deep bowls in which they kneaded the mass out of which the shewbread was made, the spoons for censers since the same word elsewhere is always represented as filled with incense, the covers for a tankard in which pure wine was kept for libations poured out every sabbath when the bread was changed, and the bowls, from a root meaning to clear away, for either the sieves by which the Levites cleansed the wheat or the ovens in which the bread was baked or vessels dipped into the tankard to draw out the wine.

Ellicott answers the same four from monuments rather than roots, the dishes probably large bowls in which the loaves were brought to the table, such bowls being common in the Egyptian wall decorations, the so-called spoons small pots in which the incense was put and burnt, two of which appear on the Arch of Titus, and the covers and bowls flagons and chalices for the drink offerings; and on the closing clause he prefers the margin, to pour out withal rather than to cover withal.

Gill says of the dishes only that the shewbread loaves were set upon them, and adds a rabbinic detail that they were of the form of the bread and of two sorts, one of gold and one of iron, the bread being baked in the iron one and put into the golden one until the morrow of the sabbath.

debates.question: What were the four vessels?
debates.positions: Clarke works from the Hebrew roots and reaches kneading bowls, censers, a wine tankard and either sieves or ovens; Ellicott works from Egyptian wall decorations and the carving on the Arch of Titus and reaches serving bowls, incense pots, flagons and chalices; they agree on the censers and differ on nearly everything else.

debates.question: Does the last clause mean to cover or to pour out?
debates.positions: Ellicott prefers the marginal reading, to pour out withal, on the ground that drink offerings were poured out in libation; the received text and the other witnesses keep to cover withal.

outliers.view: Passes on the tradition that the grain for the shewbread was sowed, reaped, ground, sifted, kneaded and baked by the Levites themselves, and takes one of the vessels to be the sieves used in that work.

schools.summary: Clarke explains the name two ways without choosing, either because the loaves were placed before the presence or face of God in the sanctuary or because they were made square, probably cubes with each side presenting the same appearance, though the Hebrew text seems to him to intimate the first since the Lord says they were set before my face; he adds that a golden dish of frankincense stood on the top of each row and was burned as a memorial when the loaves were changed; and he refuses to add a conjecture of his own about their meaning, holding it more difficult to ascertain than almost any other emblem in the whole Jewish economy.

Gill describes the arrangement, twelve cakes in two rows standing a whole week and renewed every sabbath, the old ones eaten by the priests, and reads them as a memorial of the goodness of God in daily providing bread for Israel and, since the priests ate them, as expressive of the communion between God and them; he also takes the unleavened cakes for the purity and sincerity of the church and the number twelve for the whole spiritual Israel.

Ellicott gives the name simply as bread of face or bread of presence; Keil and Delitzsch are more careful about the direction of the gift, that the loaves lay before the face of God as a meat-offering presented by the children of Israel, not as food for God but as a symbol of the spiritual food Israel was to prepare, the bread and wine as the fruit of its labour on the soil of its inheritance being a symbol of its spiritual labour in the kingdom of God.

debates.question: Why is it called bread of faces?
debates.positions: Clarke offers the choice between a placing before the face of God and a square shape with faces on every side, and leans to the first on the wording of the verse; Gill and Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch all take it as presence without entertaining the other.

debates.question: What did the bread represent?
debates.positions: Gill makes it a memorial of daily providence and a token of communion, since the priests ate what had been set before God; Keil and Delitzsch reverse the direction and make it a gift from Israel rather than food for God, a symbol of the spiritual labour it owed in the kingdom of God; Clarke declines to answer at all and will not add to the conjectures already made.

outliers.view: Refuses to conjecture, holding the use of the shewbread more difficult to ascertain than almost any other emblem in the whole Jewish economy, and preferring the older account that the tabernacle was God house and these were simply the furnishings of it.

schools.summary: Clarke describes the form as one shaft with six branches, seven lamps in all lighted every evening and extinguished every morning, and claims an unusual certainty about it, since the candlestick and the golden table and the silver trumpets were carried in triumph to Rome after the overthrow of Jerusalem and are sculptured on the arch that records it, a correct model of which stood before him as he wrote.

Henry adds that it was solid and not hollow and divides its qualities, magnificent and a great ornament to the place, and convenient, contrived both to scatter the light and to keep the tabernacle clean of smoke and snuffs; and he joins Wesley in reading the absence of windows as a statement about the age, that all its light was candle-light, which intimates the comparative darkness of that dispensation.

Ellicott corrects the three terms to cups, pomegranates and blossoms, notes that the cups are afterwards said to be like almond blossoms, and insists that all was of one piece with the stem and branches; Keil and Delitzsch gloss each word, the base, the reed or hollow stem, cups resembling the calix of a flower, spherical knobs and flowers in the form of buds.

Gill notes that it was another piece of household furniture, useful especially in a house with no windows, stood in the holy place on the south side opposite the table, and holds forth the light put into it since it has none of itself.

debates.question: What do the names of the ornaments mean?
debates.positions: Ellicott renders them cups, pomegranates and blossoms and ties the cups to almond blossoms; Keil and Delitzsch give cups resembling a flower calix, spherical knobs and bud-shaped flowers; Clarke describes six flowers like lilies with bowls and knops placed alternately.

outliers.view: Turns the Roman triumph into a lament and then answers himself, that to see these sacred articles gracing the triumph of a heathen emperor and at last consecrated to an idol affords melancholy reflections, though they had by then accomplished the end for which they were instituted, the true light being come.

themes: the comparative darkness of that dispensation

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch build the candlestick up from the base more exactly than anyone else, three side pipes branching from the central stem on either side and curving upwards in a quadrant to its level, four calices with knob and blossom on the stem and three on each branch, a knob wherever the arms branched off, the whole combined so as to form one piece of beaten work; they also report and reject an explanation which takes the words for knob and flower as in apposition, so that the flower-cups would consist of knobs with flowers bursting from them, since the opening verse names cups, knobs and flowers as three separate things; Ellicott leaves open whether the three cups on a branch were consecutive or each held a pomegranate followed by a blossom, and prefers the latter.

Gill passes on a rabbinic detail of scale, that two branches were drawn out from the middle of the knop on either side and that the height of the whole was eighteen hands breadth; Calvin reads the seven lights as a lesson about how God is to be worshipped, that a light was set before their eyes which might disperse all the darkness of error, lest they should obscure his worship with their gross inventions.

debates.question: Were the cups, knobs and flowers three things or one?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch report the view that the words stand in apposition so that a flower-cup would be a knob with a flower bursting from it, and reject it both as a singular idea and because the opening verse names the three separately; Ellicott treats them as distinct and asks only whether they ran consecutively along a branch or in repeated groups.

outliers.view: Reads the lamps as a warning against ceremonial religion, that the Israelites held fast the external form of the Law and were nevertheless degenerate, conceiving in obedience to their carnal reason that religion consisted in ceremonies.

themes: six branches out of the sides
one beaten work of pure gold

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the Hebrew idiom for the lamps, notes that each branch as well as the stem was to have its own and that the Roman monument shows them as hemispherical bowls, describes the instruments as pincers for trimming the wicks and dishes for receiving what was removed, and reports the spread of estimates for the gold talent, none placing it much below four thousand pounds while some carry it as high as ten or eleven thousand; Keil and Delitzsch convert the talent to Parisian grains, remark that a candlestick of very considerable size was possible from that quantity, and pass on a conjecture matching its height to the table.

Gill counts the seven lamps and takes them for the gifts and graces of the Spirit or the ministers of the Gospel, collects the rabbinic guesses about the instruments including vessels full of water into which the snuffings were dropped so that they might not smoke, gives the common talent at sixty pounds and the sacred at double, and reads the closing charge strictly, that nothing was left to the will, humour and fancy of men; Calvin insists that no mere vision is in question but that the external ornaments have their spiritual object.

Clarke works out the value of the talent at length from the half-shekels the people contributed, and reads the closing verse as a command issued after the whole description was finished, which he then turns into a rule for the Church, that as God gave the plan by which the tabernacle must be constructed so he gives the doctrines by which the Christian Church is to be modelled.

debates.question: What was a talent of gold worth?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch convert it to eight hundred and twenty-two thousand Parisian grains without pricing it; Gill reports one bishop reckoning at over five thousand pounds; Clarke works the same bishop figures from the half-shekels and reaches six thousand seven hundred and fifty; Ellicott declines a figure and reports a range from four thousand to eleven thousand.

debates.question: What is the force of the closing charge about the pattern?
debates.positions: Gill reads it as strictness about workmanship, that nothing was left to the will, humour and fancy of men; Calvin reads it as a claim about the vision, that its object was spiritual and not a mere spectacle; Clarke reads it forward into the Church, as the ground for holding fast a form of sound words.

outliers.view: Takes the closing verse as the model for an apostolic charge, holding that the Apostle had this command in view when he told his son in the faith to hold fast the form of sound words he had heard of him.

themes: after their pattern in the mount
